books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — The Jungle and the Meat-packing Industry
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Verbatim excerpt (abridged) from the Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906, public domain.
stimulus.text: For the purposes hereinbefore set forth the Secretary shall cause to be made, by inspectors appointed for that purpose, an examination and inspection of all cattle, sheep, swine, and goats before they shall be allowed to enter into any slaughtering, packing, or canning establishment... and said inspectors shall have access at all times, by day or night, whether the establishment be operated or not, to every part of said establishment; and said inspectors shall mark, stamp, tag, or label as 'Inspected and passed' all such products found to be not adulterated. — Federal Meat Inspection Act, 1906 (abridged)

options.misconception: The packers opposed inspection; the push came from readers disgusted by Sinclair's descriptions, not from packers fearing rivals.
Vegetarianism played no role; readers wanted clean meat, not no meat.

options.text: reformers worried about the power of urban political machines
options.misconception: Machine politics was a separate Progressive target; the meat act answered disgust at dirty packing plants.

rationales.A: Sinclair's The Jungle described filthy conditions in Chicago's packing plants, and readers were disgusted. Roosevelt had the claims investigated, confirmed them, and pushed Congress to pass the Meat Inspection Act.
rationales.B: The packers fought inspection. The pressure came from the reading public, not from the industry.
rationales.C: Nobody in 1906 was passing meat laws because of vegetarianism. Readers wanted meat they could trust.
rationales.D: Political machines ran cities; they did not run packing plants. The meat act answered the packers, not the bosses.
rationales.general:
1. Ask what moved Congress in 1906. A bestselling novel had just shown readers the inside of a packing plant.
2. Follow the chain. Sinclair's descriptions disgusted the public, Roosevelt investigated, and Congress passed the act.
3. Rule out the other worries. Packers, vegetarians, and machine reformers did not drive this law.
Remember: a book can move a law when it shows readers something they cannot unsee, so trace the law back to the book that exposed the problem.
